items.body: Review by FalconBleck — #59 ReviewI found this one because of a certain vocalist from another prog rock band that I love, any recentsurprise is welcome, I'm sure that I haven't heard everything in the Genesis world, is just that Istruggle finding new things to hear, and this was and is what I needed.- Watcher Of The Skies (Hush): Already an interesting proposal with a different sound, then adifferent introduction that starts with the chords, and then the main riff in acoustic guitar soundsgreat, then in familiar territory, but still very modern, it works really good for a new version ofthe song, no complaints, I'm sure that I come back to this version from time to time, well doneHush.- Firth Of Fifth (Over The Garden Wall): Very similar to the original, barely any difference, doneas faithful as it can be, as much as I like how it sounds, I sometimes feel like I would ratherlisten to the original, since they are so similar, but at the same time, they are so similar thatthis version can satisfy me from listening to the original. There are subtle differences, thekeyboard middle part is done with an acoustic guitar, at least the main part, then it goes back tokeyboard, it sounds great, but again, so similar, honestly well done, the quality on this album hasbeen great so far. Ok, people want to know about the guitar solo, some people only seem to careabout that, I get it, its great, but there's more song to be enjoyed, anyways, the solo is like amix between Steve and Daryl, that's also great, a very well done Firth Of Fifth.- Undertow (Jay Tausig): Continuing with quality and versions being very similar, this one is reallyclose again, however, this one sounds a bit more melancholic, the voice has less power than Phil,its like closer to Tony Banks, and he made the song, add to this the faded keyboards, and you have aversion that feels more melancholic. The piano sound is also more up-front, I keep coming back tothis version for those slight differences.- Ripples (Annie Haslam): I found this album through this song, the vocalist of Renaissance playinga Genesis song? I have to listen to this, and then I found that it was Ripples, least to say myexpectations were very high. Then I heard it, and at first it was everything I expected, she doesher own spin into the song and sounds great, however, no solo, instead a more happy version of thesong, that I kind of dig, but at the same time, I would like to hear Annie singing over the originalinstrumental done by Genesis, at least this is the closest we can get.- Back in NYC (Kevin Gilbert): Kind of prophetic in a way, Genesis did a lighter version of TheLamb, and this one starts like that, then it obviously goes back to being the usual song, there wasmaybe a need for this to be 2 versions, but it doesn't matter, the song introduces some new ideas,the quiet parts are more quiet, and sometimes even funky, it really plays more with thejuxtaposition of moods that the original song introduces, and while I like the vocals and what's inhere, I still want to listen to the original more, and the ending with the NYC atmosphere issomething I truly don't like, just stop the song beforethat comes.- For Absent Friends (Richard Sinclair): I really admire this version of the song, the vocals areendearing, the instrumentation feels richer with the added strings and harpsichord, and if thatwasn't enough, the song gets extended to almost twice its length, this is definitely a must listenfrom this album. - Mama (Magellan): I like how the drum pattern sounds, most of it gets respected, however, I'm notsure about the rest of the sounds, for a moment the song is just fine, the introduction is fast,which is nice, but then the first laugh gets ruined by an uninspired drum roll, the voice justdoesn't get there, for some reason the notes are all high as soon as possible, it just doesn't work,its as if they wanted to be louder than the original just for the sake of it. Finally we reach thelaugh, and again, its too much, the point of the song is that it was simple and tense, if you wantedto add more into the song, it would've been a good idea to hear the pre-release version, however, itwasn't released back then yet. I will just say, for a moment it was very promising, production isgood, I have no doubt that these are good musicians, just obviously not Genesis.- Man Of Our Times (Enchant): I usually don't mention production, because my copy of the CD could bethe problem, well, I'm listening from YT, and this one sounds weak for some reason, like its lackingsomething, but that's probably the upload, ignoring all that, this version is very comparable to theoriginal, except for everything that sounds a bit weaker, the strongs are the over-drive guitar andthe background voices that sound louder than in the original, that also do a more noticeablefun stereo play, which is a production win. Honestly, this version is fine, but I would ratherlisten to the original, there's nothing that makes me comeback to this version because its sosimilar, the over-drive doesn't convince me.- Many Too Many (Peter Bardens): One advantage this version has over the original is that the firstincrease is more subtle, and the second is bigger, while in the original both feel similar, however,the original has a very cool guitar solo that's heavily reduced in this version, that could've beena very neat improvement.- Entangled (Shadow Gallery): Incredibly similar to the original, well done instrumental, the voiceson the chorus though sound like the three musketeers, it doesn't work and it takes me away from thesong. The guitars sound very clean and pleasant, the ending is not as strong, yet very close,overall a good version that feels new, it just needs to fix the chorus. Minus points for the fade-out instead of having an ending.- Squonk (Cairopaiva): There are some decisions I don't like, the instruments seem to alternatebetween ideas that don't work well, they add things that could be welcome, but they aren't cleverenough, they feel out of place, the guitar at the start, the drums a bit after that, the best thingabout this song is the voice, the vocalist does a very good job, sounds fresh and respectful, hefits the song well enough, which is surprising by how difficult it is. The ending is ruined here,why do you have talking, and a very early fade-out? Terrible decision.- I Know What I Like (Crack The Sky): What is this? Crack The Sky? They are great, but what was theidea here? Being different just for the sake of it? It doesn't fit the rest of this album as well,its so weird, but I kind of dig the style change, it sounds more scary than happy, I think that'ssomething good, but other than that, this is just a curiosity, they managed something veryinteresting here, it doesn't sound like anything on this album, or Crack The Sky, or any decisionthat Genesis would've taken with this song, but it still sounds a bit like Genesis, its so weird.- The Carpet Crawlers (Michael Zentner): I'm sorry, the voice doesn't do it for me, its too forced,the kind of forced voice you get away with in high school, like no one told you that it wasn't good.This is sadly one of worst Carpet Crawlers I have heard so far, I'm sorry for being so harsh, Ireally don't like it, the drums are too loud an static, the strings are barely here and I completelymiss the keyboard I love so much, the guitar is fine, but not enough... This is definitely a CarpetCrawlers, but its just so under-cooked, and the single voice is over-done, totally missing the pointof the song. The best I can say that it seems to be a respectful attempt, although the forced voicefeels like a mockery at times, I just can't recommend this one.- Keep It Dark (World Trade): Now this one is weaker, but it respects even the smallest details atthe best it can, however, it really lacks an stronger bass and keyboards, the voice is fine,obviously not Phil, but its well done. The differences are so small that they barely matter, andalso the song ends faster, well done but not enough.In conclusion, this album is a bit of a mix bag, there are some interesting proposals and even someideas that can be good to listen as a new version that compliments the original, however, I don'tthink that any of these versions represent the best of what this artists can do, I appreciate theeffort a lot and the amount of Genesis eras that they covered, I'm glad that this exists, I justwish that it was better and that it had a better name, because some of what's in here needs to beheard by Genesis and prog rock fans.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张1995年发行的Genesis致敬合辑，收录了多位艺术家对Genesis经典曲目的翻唱。评论涉及《Watcher Of The Skies》《Firth Of Fifth》《Undertow》《Ripples》《Back in NYC》等曲目，其中Annie Haslam（Renaissance主唱）参与了演绎。整体而言，这些翻唱版本大多忠实于原作，编曲上仅有细微差异，键盘段落改为原声吉他等调整，并无突破性的实验性改造或前卫声响设计。该专辑属于主流前卫摇滚领域的致敬作品，与实验/先锋、学院派爵士、电子、世界融合、暗潮及当代古典等方向距离较远，缺乏原创性和跨类型深度融合。

items.excerpt: New Orleans-raised alto saxophonist Jesse Davis, 40 years into his career, reflects on his journey following his 60th birthday with a new album, Reflections (Cellar Music).
items.body:
Jesse Davis Rediscovers Joy

New Orleans-raised alto saxophonist Jesse Davis, 40 years into his career, reflects on his journey following his 60th birthday with a new album, Reflections (Cellar Music). The album represents a homecoming — both musically and personally — as Davis reconnects with the joy of playing jazz.

Quote: "Forty years into this career, I have come back to myself, and I feel the same joy I did the first time I opened that sax case every time I play."

Albums as bandleader: 10. Key collaborators: Clark Terry, Ray Brown, Milt Jackson, Benny Golson. 1980s prominence as part of the "young lions" movement spearheaded by Wynton Marsalis.

The Album: Reflections (Cellar Music)
- "Blue Autumn" — sprightly, Latin-influenced opener exploring grief
- "Choctaw Alley" — blues-inflected, evokes New Orleans roots
- "Reflections" — Monk standard
- "Evidence" — Monk standard

Musicians: Jesse Davis (alto sax), Spike Wilner (piano), John Webber (bass), Lewis Nash (drums)
items._cn_summary: Jesse Davis的《Reflections》是一张回归传统主流爵士风格的中音萨克斯四重奏专辑。音乐内容以Monk经典曲目翻奏为主，辅以拉丁风格与新奥尔良布鲁斯元素，整体属于温故知新型的'青年雄狮'派系爵士。Davis在六十大寿之际重新发掘演奏传统爵士的喜悦，音乐语言稳健但缺乏实验性与前卫色彩。合作乐手为纽约主流爵士圈的资深演奏家，厂牌Cellar Music虽属独立小厂牌，但音乐取向与传统bebop一脉相承。整篇乐评信息偏短，更接近艺人动态简讯而非深度评论。对于偏好实验爵士、自由即兴、电子声响或暗潮工业等前卫路线的听众而言，此专辑在风格取向上与之距离较远。

items.body:
Larry McCray's Heartbreak City, released on Keeping the Blues Alive Records, is steeped in grit, anguish, resilience and hard-won joy. The album reflects the life of a working-class blues man who sharpened his craft in the clubs of Saginaw after shifts on the General Motors assembly line, before touring nationally and eventually across Europe with Albert Collins. Every track carries the emotional weight of decades spent earning success the hard way, drawing deeply from McCray's Arkansas roots while sounding fully grounded in the modern blues tradition.

"Try to Be a Good Man," co-written by McCray, serves as both introduction and mission statement. Riding a chugging roadhouse groove—with a bright, punctuating all-star horn section featuring Dan Fornero, Wayne Bergeron, Andy Martin and Sal Lozano—the song doubles as advice for younger men navigating relationships. McCray's baritone, earthy, warm and unforced, anchors lines such as: "Give her all the love you can and do your best to understand." His guitar work is concise and expressive, delivering sharp, brittle, conversational bends that echo the influence of Little Milton without slipping into imitation. The performance highlights one of McCray's defining strengths: emotional honesty delivered without theatrics.

The title track provides the album's emotional center. Built on a deep blues-rock pocket shaped by the modern production style associated with producers Joe Bonamassa and Josh Smith, "Heartbreak City" unfolds with the restless momentum of an open highway. McCray's stinging guitar lines recall Albert King, while his vocal phrasing again nods to Milton. The song captures the album's defining theme: a man worn down by loss, disappointment and the daily grind, yet still unwilling to surrender. It is weary and determined at the same time, balancing vulnerability with quiet resolve.

On "Everything Falls on Me," McCray channels his frustration through a mid-tempo blues-rock groove shaped by Bo Diddley-style syncopation and terse, declarative guitar figures reminiscent of Chuck Berry. Its lyrics about carrying everyone else's burdens strike a familiar chord without lapsing into self-pity. "When it comes to disaster, Red Cross got nothin' on me / I've cleaned up more messes than the human eye can see / Be it friend or family or someone I just met / They only hit me up for something, anything they can get." McCray sings with a convincing authority that transforms everyday frustrations into something universal.

McCray's songwriting strengths surface again in "Bye Bye Blues," co-written with Charlie Walmsley and nominated for Song of the Year at the 2026 Blues Music Awards. Built around the line, "When I said hello to you, I said goodbye to the blues," the song balances classic blues sentiment with understated optimism and demonstrates McCray's ability to write memorable, emotionally direct material.

Throughout Heartbreak City, McCray honors the artists who shaped him while remaining unmistakably himself. Positioned somewhere between Albert King's fire and Little Milton's silky soulfulness, he delivers performances defined by warmth, grit and emotional clarity. In an era still searching for towering modern blues voices, McCray makes a compelling case for his place near the top of the genre's current generation.

Try To Be A Good Man; Heartbreak City; Bye Bye Blues; Bright Side; Everything Falls On Me; I Know What I Have Done; Keep On Loving My Baby; Hangman; Stop Your Crying; Crazy World.

The Kirk Fletcher Band

Additional Instrumentation

Kirk Fletcher: Guitar on "Bright Side," "Bye Bye Blues" and "Keep On Loving My Baby"; Dan Fornero: Flugelhorn; Wayne Bergeron: Flugelhorn; Andy Martin: Bass Trombone; Sal Lozano: Baritone Saxophone, Flutes.

items.body: Review by AFlowerKingCrimson — This band has a sound that's rather hard to pin down. Overall, they are rather laid back and not very intense or heavy which can be a good thing if you just want something to relax to or at least something that is not metallish or too heavy. There are some elements that might bring to mind Pink Floyd and apparently on their subsequent albums there's a bit of a Dire Straits element (there's a little bit of that on here too but not much-mostly in some of the guitar sounds).Some of this has saxophone and there's also some flute, violin and cello. Also, much of this is rather "normal" sounding rock with maybe a bit of a roots rock or even a mild blues rock element (maybe that's where the Dire Straits comparisons come in). The first track, Pilgrim, which is in three secions is maybe the best thing on here but there are other fine moments as well. "From the Mist Rows the Bard" is nice also. However, I must say I'm not too keen on the fact that there are different lead vocalists on here and I'm especially not much of a fan of the singer with the rough raspy sounding voice. Just one singer and especially someone with a smoother voice would be more appreciated by me. Still, I wouldn't say it ruins the music and ultimately it's probably just a personal preference on my point. Overall, this is nothing earth shattering but it's a nice release. It's also rather short at 37 minutes and some change. It doesn't quite reach four stars for me but I'll give it 3.5. A nice album with some good Pink Floydish moments.

Tensions soar among BTS ARMY in Singapore as scalpers & resellers emerge during 'ARIRANG' tour ticket sales

The great ticket wars have begun as BTS' ARMY in Singapore warm up their fast fingers in hopes of catching their favourites live after a gruelling seven-year wait. As one of the most anticipated live concert events of the year, fans are desperate to get their hands on tickets to one of the four nights of the BTS WORLD TOUR ‘ARIRANG’ IN SINGAPORE.

However, their enemies have also entered the battlefield: scalpers. Modern ticketing culture has seen the rapid rise of scalpers snatching tickets away from die-hard fans, using numerous bots to create fake accounts and bypass ticket purchase limits and queue numbers. The scalpers then upsell the tickets on reselling sites for ludicrous prices, luring fans who are desperate for a chance to catch their favourite act live.

As of today, 3 June, the ARMY membership presale has taken place. In order to buy tickets, fans were required to sign up for an ARMY MEMBERSHIP (GLOBAL) on Weverse to get the exclusive promo code. However, one fan took advantage of this, selling access to their code on Carousell for $20.

That's not all, others have even gone to lengths such as multiplying the original ticket prices up to a whopping 23 times when listing the tickets on the online reselling site StubHub. Originally, VIP tickets were priced at $388 on Ticketmaster, while on StubHub, they shot up to about $8,969, a significant jump from the originally listed prices.

Beyond Carousell and StubHub, one fan even took to X to promote the sale of the tickets she had scalped, with fans in the comments expressing their outrage. The tweet showed screenshots of a Google Sheet populated with rows and rows of available tickets, prices, and seat locations. Some of the tickets were bundled with seats positioned next to each other. ARMYs in the comments did not hold back, with some of them going on to comment things like, "@TicketmasterSG this person is a scalper who ruined so many real fans out of their tickets. Please invalidate their tickets" and "Can you handle this pls? This is unfair for the armys @TicketmasterSG @TicketmasterCS".

Ahead of today's ticket wars, Singapore Police Force (SPF) and Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) warned ARMYs about scams, advising them to only purchase tickets from authorised sellers. CASE president Melvin Yong cautioned fans that resold tickets may even be voided by ticket service providers. He added, "Purchasing tickets from unauthorised sources may therefore expose consumers not only to the risk of scams, but also the possibility of being denied entry to the event."

As excitement for BTS' long-awaited return to Singapore continues to reach fever pitch, fans are being urged to remain vigilant and exercise caution when purchasing tickets. While the battle for seats may be fierce, authorities and consumer groups alike stress that buying only through authorised channels remains the safest way to secure a place at the highly anticipated concerts. With additional presales and general sales still ahead, many ARMYs are hoping perseverance, rather than paying inflated resale prices, will be the key to seeing BTS live once again.

'ANH TRAI "SAY HI" - DAY 9: REPLY 2024' brings the heat after overwhelming fan support — gig report
SPINS
630
Estimated: 
4 mins
 reading
Words by Sharvamaya Mohan
First published:
3 June 2026
Last updated:
3 June 2026
NEWS
GIGS
MUSIC
EVENTS

Back in 2024, Anh trai ‘Say Hi’ commanded the spotlight with ease as the music reality TV show, created and produced by DatVietVAC Group Holdings, staged eight monumental concerts in Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, and two in Las Vegas.

In response to the incredible enthusiasm fans showed throughout the reality series, ANH TRAI "SAY HI" - DAY 9: REPLY 2024, which took place on 18 April at Vạn Phúc City, was a heartfelt thank-you to those who supported the show every step of the way. As the Vietnamese pop scene continues to grow, artists in that scene continue to branch out and evolve to put their region's greatest talents on the map, step onto global stages, and spread the joy that flows through their authentic artistry.

Background of the show

When the announcement for the anticipated ninth concert was first unveiled back in March by Vie Concerts fanpage on Threads, fans expressed their excitement, breaking records with the platform’s trending rankings rising to over two million mentions in the following 12 hours. This ninth show reignites the show's immense popularity as it has continued to smash ratings since its debut in 2024.

Anh trai ‘Say Hi’ translates to "Say Hi Never Say Goodbye" and it follows 30 musical talents who are referred to as brothers. In each episode, they participate in challenges and competitions to refine their artistry and become a member of the final band lineup that features the best contestants. Becoming an instant hit, the series has garnered over 18 billion views online, with many of its performances going viral across YouTube, Spotify, and iTunes, and sparking widespread conversation on social media.

Fans often showcased their unwavering support for participants and the show itself as they travelled from abroad to attend concerts and even organise fan events, building a positive and sizable fandom for the show. Due to the show becoming a cultural phenomenon, it quickly earned recognition from the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism as a leading performance programme of 2024 and one of the Top 10 cultural, sports, and tourism events of the year.

The show's outstanding structure and wide reach earned it several awards, such as digital phenomenon of the year at the Vietnam iContent Awards 2024, Golden Apricot Blossom Award, Green Wave 2024, and the title of entertainment phenomenon of the year at Star of the Year 2024.

Gig report

28 of the 30 "brothers" transformed Vạn Phúc City into a high-octane celebration of Vietnamese pop and boundary-breaking musicality. Despite the absence of Anh Tú Atus and Quang Trung due to scheduling conflicts, the remaining talents turned up the heat, delivering the energetic performances the audience had been eagerly awaiting.

The members truly "Never Say Goodbye" as the show was packed with a nostalgic setlist of songs. They opened the concert with a heartfelt promise by performing 'Say Hi Never Say Goodbye.' The show unfolded with Live Stage one that saw the explosive renditions of songs such as 'Hút,' 'Don't Care,' 'Bảnh,' 'ICON,' and 'No Far, No Star.' Live Stage two, on the other hand, brought the vibrant soundscapes of 'You Had Me at Hello,' 'Poet,' 'Love Sand,' 'Halo,' and 'Catch Me If You Can.'

Rounding off the performances, Live Stage three took a more introspective turn with evocative lyrics and wistful melodies in songs like 'REGRET', 'Ngáo ngơ', and 'Cứ để anh ta rời đi'. Fan favourites such as 'The Minute and the Hour', along with performances of 'It’s All Yours', 'Sincere', and 'Walk', created memorable singalong moments for the audience.

Hai Dang Doo, NICKY, Song Luan, Gin Tuan Kiet, and Vu Thinh also brought an amusing twist to 'How to Love the Right Way', featured in You're Beautiful Say Hi. As the final beats of 'A-list Stars' and 'The Stars' reverberated through the venue, the show brought the journey full circle and left a lasting impression on the audience.

Although there was some controversy surrounding the slow ticket sales and changes to the stage location that were being discussed on social media, fans still undoubtedly had a blast during the show.

The overwhelming excitement from fans is a testament to the show's enduring impact, proving that its music, performances, and sense of community continue to resonate long after its original run. As the franchise prepares to return to the stage, the ninth concert promises to be another landmark moment in the ongoing success story of one of Vietnam's most influential entertainment phenomena.

Following the exciting announcement that CORTIS will be joining the shimmering lineup for Lollapalooza Chicago 2026, they are ready to chart their own path and share their unique punk-tinged K-pop flair. This August, the quintet is set to embark on their first-ever 2026 CORTIS TOUR IN NORTH AMERICA, taking them across six cities in the region.

Fresh off the success of their EP GREENGREEN, which reached No. 3 on the Billboard 200, CORTIS show no signs of slowing down. As they continue to push their artistry forward with each release, the group is rapidly emerging as one of the standout names in K-pop's new generation.

Across the six shows, they will perform in cities such as Toronto, New York, Atlanta, Irving, Los Angeles, and San Francisco.

Aug 4 — The Theatre at Great Canadian Toronto — Toronto, ON 
Aug 6 — Infosys Theater at Madison Square Garden — New York, NY 
Aug 8 — Fox Theatre — Atlanta, GA
Aug 11 — The Pavilion at Toyota Music Factory — Irving, TX 
Aug 13 — YouTube Theater — Los Angeles, CA 
Aug 15 — The Theater at Bill Graham Civic Auditorium — San Francisco, CA 

Tickets for the North American tour will first be available through the COER Membership (Global) presale on 9 June at 3 PM local time, before opening to the general public on 10 June at 3 PM local time. Fans can also elevate their concert experience with a VIP package featuring premium seating, access to a post-show CORTIS Hi-Bye event, an exclusive gift item, and additional perks. Click here for Additional ticketing and registration details. 

With their first North American tour on the horizon, CORTIS are poised to bring their high-energy performances and distinctive sound to an even wider audience. Building on the momentum of GREENGREEN and a string of major milestones, the tour marks another exciting step in the group's journey as they continue to expand their global reach and connect with fans across borders.

items.body:
The fourteen-member Hot House West Swing Orchestra, enabled by Salt Lake City, Utah's nonprofit Hot House West, makes its recorded debut with Joy in Rhythm, Vol. 1, an array of eleven danceable songs, most of which were popular during the Swing Era's golden age in the 1930s and '40s.

This is an album especially designed for dancing; it even includes a booklet that teaches the listener a number of simple dance moves tailored for beginners. In spite of the fact that there are several cursory solos along the way (the longest by violinist Curtis Woodbury), this is not a jazz album per se but one that borrows the rhythms of jazz—most notably swing—to press home its danceable message.

As a guide for dancers, Joy in Rhythm works fairly well. One can imagine a dance floor filled with men and women who are grooving to the music. Remove dancing from the equation, however, and the album reveals a number of flaws, not the least of which is the many liberties taken with the character and tempo of the original compositions—some or even all of which were no doubt deemed necessary to make the finished product more accessible to dancers.

The orchestra's vocalists, Hayley Kirkland and Nathan Royal (who doubles on lead guitar and whistling), are at least on a par with many Swing Era band singers, which can be taken as rather faint praise. As for the orchestra, in terms of power and consonance, it is somewhere below the norm when compared to working professional ensembles, which the Hot House West orchestra does not claim to be. To verify that impression, one need do no more than listen to the closing number, Count Basie's classic "One O'Clock Jump." Case closed.

As no one is likely to amass much wealth performing with this group, it is assuredly a labor of love. And that is perhaps how it should be appraised—as a heartfelt summons to dancers and would-be dancers to leave the couch, head for a ballroom and immerse themselves in the irrepressible Joy of Rhythm.

Dark Eyes; Honeysuckle Rose; I'm Gonna Sit Right Down (And Write Myself a Letter); On the Sunny Side of the Street; Katusha; Grand Terrace Rhythm; I've Got Spurs (That Jingle, Jangle, Jingle); Hit That Jive Jack; A Mellow Bit of Rhythm; Them There Eyes; One O'clock Jump

items.body:
A little over a month ago, New Delhi imprint Antariksh Records and prominent streetwear/sneaker retailers VegNonVeg joined forces to launch KISSA In-Store radio, livestreaming and archiving sets from the latter's Gurgaon store. With the aim of curating "broadcasts for the curious", the mix and radio series has featured the likes of Unnayanaa, Bombie, Farhan Rehman and flux vortex.

As part of its aim to document and archive the current alternative listening practices around sound and amplification present in the city of Delhi-NCR, and International Synthesiser Day, KISSA In-Store Radio brought together the synth communities that have been quietly growing in the capital city.

Shiv Ahuja aka Songs For A Tired City took charge of the 3-hour special, representing Synth Hang, an organically growing group of synthesiser enthusiasts which started as informal at-home gatherings but has since evolved to involve the who's who of the city's synth acts with multi-faceted interactive live events and even internationally prominent figures like Laurie Anderson paying a visit. Alongside an interview, Ahuja performed a set based around the iconic synth Buchla Easel, weaving ambient and leftfield sounds to showcase Synth Hang's penchant for the same.

Shaurya Sarin aka Imerohi has been building the live event series, Alt Baithak. While not exclusively dedicated to synthesisers, Alt Baithak also fully dedicates itself to the experimental, both in terms of sound and event flow, as it features workshops, immersive rituals and film screenings besides live sets. Imerohi builds a similar sense to his KISSA In-Store Radio set, morphine his guitar and triggering synth patterns that traverse ambient, post-rock and club music.

Lastly, Ahuja brings in Aditya Ghosh who, as Angia, builds modules for Eurorack synthesiser systems and performs music for them. Doing the same for his set, Angia offers a pacier performance where four-to-the-floor grooves are teeming with arpeggios and melodies teeming with textures that cut through.

Head here to stream more sets from KISSA In-Store Radio, and follow Antariksh Records to stay updated.

Kabir Sehgal's Community of Curiosity

Profile of Kabir Sehgal — a former finance executive turned prolific Grammy-winning music producer and creator. On Feb. 1, Sehgal received his 14th Grammy Award as producer of the audiobook Meditations: The Reflections Of His Holiness The Dalai Lama.

Notable collaborators: Ted Nash, Joe Alterman, Rufus Wainwright, Maggie Rogers, Andra Day, Arturo O'Farrill, Jonathan Batiste, Lil Jon.

Latest Release: stars and static — 10-track, 30-minute lo-fi digital meditation combining field recordings of American locales with iconic American songs.

Career: Vice president of emerging markets at J.P. Morgan, published 4th book Coined, produced 30+ albums. Now pivoting from producer to creator.

items.body:
Back on the Cutting-Edge Trail, in Victoriaville

Coverage of FIMAV (Festival du Musique Actuelle de Victoriaville), Quebec. The festival returned after near-absence the previous year under new director Scott Thomson.

Notable performances:
- Amirtha Kidambi's Elder Ones
- Darius Jones Trio
- Zubot Brothers (Joshua and Jesse)
- John Oswald's "PlunderphoniCoveralls"
- Queen Mab — Marilyn Lerner + Lori Freedman (40 years together)
- Pat Thomas solo piano and with أحمد [Ahmed]
- Rafael Toral (Portuguese electric guitarist)
- Sarah Pagé's Voda with No Hay Banda
- Eric Chenaux
- Fanfare Pourpour (20-piece ensemble)

The 20-piece ensemble Fanfare Pourpour, which began life as a guerilla street band in Montreal in the '70s, closed the festival.

items.body: Matthew Wright: Notation, Improvisation, and Technology Anton van Houten, Erik-Jan de With, Saskia Lankhoorn, Pete Harden, Neil Charles, Sofia Jernberg, Joey Marijs, Mandhira de Saram, Stephen Davis, Matthew Wright, Alexander Hawkins, Michiel van Dijk © 2026 Tessa Veldhorst & Musical Utopias “The thing about playing the tuba in an orchestra is that you don’t have to play that much,” admitted composer Matthew Wright, who grew up playing the tuba in orchestras and funk bands, “but it’s the best seat in the house. You hear music back to front. The percussion and the brass are loud, so you hear all their detail, and the strings are this kind of ethereal thing that’s off in the distance.” For the Kent-based Wright, who also improvises using turntables, samplers, and processers – most impactfully with Trance Map, his partnership with Evan Parker – this early realization nurtured a sensibility leading to the creation of immersive works that mix composition, improvisation, and technology. Cracked Glaze (False Walls) is a case in point, as it utilizes notated material – “dot music” is his good-humored term – improvisation, and Wright’s real-time sampling and processing immediately fed into surround sound, all of which he remixed for the CD. Wright’s collaborators on Cracked Glaze represent various facets of his work. Ensemble Klang, an ensemble of mostly Dutch new music virtuosi, was an early champion of Wright’s compositions. Spheric Totemic is a Wright-instigated, flexibly configured improvising group with, on this occasion, Mandhira de Saram, Alexander Hawkins, Neil Charles and Stephen Davis. Sofia Jernberg, whose Musho with Hawkins was one of the brighter lights of 2024, is new to Wright’s constellation. Historically, the conventional wisdom among exponents of freely improvised music is that the larger the group, the more apt the music will be muddied. It is a yardstick that is also prevalent among practitioners of contemporary composition. Individuality – of the improviser, of the composer – is more difficult to assert in or through a crowd. Although there are more than a dozen musicians heard on Cracked Glaze , there is no nebulous sprawl or complexity for complexity’s sake. Abstraction is tethered to figuration, the spine of the piece being a descending line that repeatedly submerges and reemerges, giving the interactions of voices clear relationships. “In a lot of the written work for ensembles there is a central concern or concerns that tend to last a long period of time, an idea that will give it structure. I’m really interested in music being a kind of surface that you can kind of hear around, so that when you are listening, you are kind of experiencing a visual kind of situation. I guess this goes back to my work with records, because records make music a physical surface, where you can put the needle anywhere. “In the improvised work, I don’t want to be the guy that says to improvisers, ‘this is how it goes.’ Improvisation, in a free context, is about distributed leadership. It’s about this beautiful thing of people saying, ‘the music could go here’ or ‘I hear the future of this music in what you’re playing,’ and the kind of listening that leads to those sorts of statements. “Having the opportunity to work with a group that is mainly readers – Ensemble Klang – and a group that is mainly improvisers – Spheric Totemic – and Sofia Jernberg, gave me the opportunity to do something I haven’t heard much in my music, to have a spine that is unfurling but is always there. It doesn’t necessarily always have to be the main focus of the piece, but it will always be there. It will structure time in a certain way; improvisers can do whatever they want to do, and the music will be as much about them as it is the spine. I was really interested in having a sort of object in the space as improvisation. It’s almost like in the visual world. You have people moving in a gallery but there’s a sculpture there. It’s in the room with you.” Another virtue of Cracked Glaze is that it is the type of work that initially seems to come out of nowhere. It smacks of singularity. However, Wright’s backstory reveals that he did not come out of nowhere, as he has a pedigree linking him to England’s most consequential institutional incubator of experimental music, as well as its most venerable, living exponent of improvised music. Both associations largely account for how Wright’s disparate interests – several of which were common among Gen Xers in their formative years but were delayed in being assimilated into experimental music – were shaped into a mature aesthetic, and yielded in Cracked Glaze an arguably definitive statement. “My experience, first of all, was writing music and playing in funk bands and small improvising groups with friends,” Wright recently explained. “But I also like writing music for people who would take it away and play it somewhere else. I might not even be there for the performance. My background took me to study at the University of Huddersfield and the Contemporary Music Festival there and the guy who set it up, Richard Steinitz. I was very lucky. It was kind of random. He was my composition teacher. So, I was very lucky to have experiences like knocking on the door for a composition lesson and Richard Steinitz saying, ‘Ah, Matt, I can’t possibly teach you right now, but meet Karlheinz,’ and the door opens and there’s this amazing composer from another generation that I had read about, but never have the opportunity to meet. “Contemporary classical music was a big part of my education, but I DJed as a kid. I was really interested at that point in the ‘80s and ‘90s when software, sampling, and DJ technology, was becoming affordable. It started showing up in people’s homes. The two things were colliding in my mind when I was a kid. The only kind of education I could get was a kind of classical education with along with jazz education and jazz theory, but it was dot music, written music. Then there was this other side was like DJ culture and all of the great heritage of Black music that DJ culture is part of, and that was a kind of informal education. “When I was a real little kid – like 12 or 13 – I made a lot of bedroom productions with a basic computer and turntable setup, really focused on instrumental hip-hop. I started to scratch around then, just watching how it was done on TV. My main inspirations were DJ Premier of Gangstarr, Terminator X of Public Enemy, and Maseo of De La Soul. When I was around 18 or 19, as a student, I DJed for a few parties, playing mainly funk, hip hop, and drum ‘n' bass. Around the same time – 1996-98 – I was in a few pop funk bands that needed a DJ, so I did a few things with beat juggling and matching the pitch of the horns with turntable scratches, etc. “In 1999 I DJed for a social event at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival and I decided to just play fragments of music that I loved at the time: The Jazz Warriors, Louis Andriessen, Loose Tubes, Squarepusher, Björk. On the basis of that weird mix, I got the call to DJ at Abbey Road for the launch of a music charity, the PRS Foundation, in 2000. That was both a social event and did indeed include some hardcore scratching. When I moved to Holland in 2002, I formed a trio with laptop artist Tom Tlalim and saxophonist Keir Neuringer – now of Irreversible Entanglements – and we played a few house parties and small gigs with our own mix of free improv and beat-based electronica. That same year the Huddersfield Festival commissioned ‘Presents from an Edited Then’ which was a 70-minute piece for sax quartet and me DJing, designed for a club venue, again a mix of social and scratching. That’s when I got interested in the worlds of contemporary classical music and DJ culture colliding.” One of the first projects Wright embarked on this goal was to compose for turntables and to teach classical trained percussionists how to use them, integrating John Cage’s early work for percussion with the innovations of Christian Marclay and Otomo Yoshihide. “I have literally written out all of the material for percussionists who are readers,” Wright said of the work. “If you look at a musical stave with the four spaces between the lines, I use those spaces to represent the four spaces on a vinyl record. The space that would be a F in the treble stave, that’s the space on the outer edge of the record, before any material appears on the vinyl record. All of the material on the record is included in the second space, and then the space at the center of the record, and then the label itself in the fourth space. You can prepare those spaces, put stickers on them. I would literally write percussion rhythms and they could produce those rhythms by dropping the needle on the record and get a ricochet effect or specify a section of the record I want to be played, say a saxophone three minutes into the record. I developed these techniques where the needle sticks like a locked groover. And your basic scratching, forward and backward hand movements, so I could actually teach the basics of hip hop scratching to percussionists, even though the music didn’t sound anything like hip hop.” Wright then began to assess the proportions of and the relationships between the elements of his aesthetic and how to integrate them in his work. “ Cracked Glaze is a collision of all of the above. I have been doing ensemble work and turntable work and installation work, but a lot of my focus is on the work with Evan in mixing and even post-production of the Trance Map material. Post-production is really part of the process, and Evan is very interested in exploring all that. Although Cracked Glaze doesn’t involve Evan, it brings to equal terms all of the sources I work with. There’s some notation written for Ensemble Klang with holes in that notation, space for the improvisation group Spheric Totemic I set up with UK players like Alexander Hawkins and Neil Charles. They have start and stop times for the improvising, and they also sometimes have cues for notation as well. And I’m mixing them live on stage, as well, taking samples of them and remixing them and using the turntable as well. Then I take all that material and work on it a little in the studio, not to radically change the piece but bring out some of the elements that you would hear live but not on the recording, because it was performed with surround sound. The piece brings together notation, improvisation, and technology, but not as separate forms. They all intersect. That’s where they all join on the map.” In a roundabout way, the title of the piece speaks to the processes of its creation. It refers to the glazes used in high-fire ceramics that are formulated to crack on temperature; even though they are applied in an even manner, the cracking results in a surface that can be likened to a mosaic assembled with random tiles, with dark, hair-thin spaces between them. Though the results are subject to a unique firing, the experienced artist knows how to promote cracking that is pleasing and avoid cracking that ruins the piece. “It may be interesting to talk about how jazz standards have worked in the past,” Wright responded to the idea of controlled cracking, and chuckling at the notion that he controlled the gas valve. “An excellent standard is one that can be played in its entirety and feel integrated and beautiful, but it is also a catalyst. It offers itself up to be cracked, to be turned into something new. In some ways, the use of notation to suggest response is fascinating to me. On a technical level, there are definitely moments where I say to the improvisers, ‘at a certain point you will hear a line and at that point, that pitch, that’s your moment;’ if you’re improvising, the natural ebb and flow of the group will go to you. I don’t say ‘you should crack it’ to them; it’s yours. “And there’s a third element there, the equivalent of the heat – the processing and the spatialization. I’m taking the feed of everybody, the notated music and the improvised music is coming to my setup, and I’m able to remix it and sample it. I’m an agent in the cracking, too. Whether it is notated or not is not the point, because it’s all going through the same system and being splintered by going into surround sound. That’s the third element, a catalytic element.” Wright pointed to a poster in his studio of a still influential Japanese textile exhibition he attended in his early 20s. “What I loved about that,” he said, “was that the dynamic shapes on these textiles are very rigid, spatially, but the textiles themselves have all sorts of holes in them. They are almost like fishing nets. I tried to create something similar by creating a structure that’s flexible but is repeatable. If we play this piece again, the melody line and the structure is going to be exactly the same every time and the improvising and the specialization will be different every time. That’s a long-winded way of saying I tried not to over notate.” Wright acknowledged that post-production, particularly when the work was created in a surround sound environment and is remixed for stereo, creates a distinct experience of the work, and perhaps represents a new iteration of the pursuit of perfection in the studio, exemplified by Glenn Gould. “Pieces are concepts that have a sort of quantum existence,” Wright maintained. “What I mean is that if we are going to present the piece live, then there are circumstances that will be dynamic for the audience in the live space that may not be so dynamic hearing it at home. In the live space, I’m dealing with surround sound. There are a whole lot of options to try to present that sort of experience in the stereo format. When it comes to making a CD or something online that people will listen to, I consider the domestic setting. I also consider that many people listen to music on the go, with headphones or their phone. You may be walking down the Avenue of the Americas and everything around you is changing, but there’s one consistent thread in the music. “You have to consider the multiple ways that people listen now. I do hope that people will sit at home to listen to it. In that situation, it’s much closer to reading a book because it’s a solitary experience. You’re sitting with it for 40 or 50 minutes. Wearing headphones creates an interior experience. I really treasure those kinds of listeners and it’s a real privilege when someone spends that time with something that I’ve made with colleagues. “In the history of improvised music there has been many vehement statements about the relationship between free improvised music and recording. I totally get that, but I suppose that the question we now have to consider is what happens when you improvise with a recording. We don’t want the karaoke thing. How does the recording come back into the improvised music experience in as fluid a way you would have with another musician with an instrument? An instrument is obviously a technology of its own. The recording is the result of the technology. We need to make sure the technology is as flexible as any other instrument. The other thing I’m really fascinated by in the history of free creative music is the evolution of incorporating electronics. We are in a period where a lot of improvised music has an electronic element. You can ask the question of when and where did this music happen. Even if the music is live, happening right in front of you, like the pure, Derek Bailey way improvised music should be, an electro-acoustic situation suggests that the music is not happening in the present tense. That’s one thing working with recordings can do, present another side of the same project. “The thing I’m really interested in is those previously separated camps of notation, improvisation, and technology becoming one and the same, where there is an equaling out of the three. You’re not relying on one form of expression. And this will cause a real revitalization of the scene, where people are mastering their separate disciplines and are also negotiating with each other. It’s almost like the beginning of creative music, when people were negotiating how to reinvestigate their instrument and the music. I think there’s more opportunities for creative music because of the dialogue between notation, improvisation, and technology. Looking for the connections between them is the main creative impetus. It’s not paper; it’s not technology; it’s not adherence to one way of making music. It’s about thinking about the connections between the people you’re working with. ‘All of the above’ may be too easy an answer, but it does ascribe equal value. These are all zones on the map and they all overlap each other, so the paths are what I’m interested in.” *** Wright’s projects frequently overlap, the post production of one coinciding with the development of another. With summer approaching, Wright was mixing a duo session with Pat Thomas that has the flavor of This is Trickster ; a Spheric Totemic album, and a Trance Map + recording on which Parker and him are joined by harpist Milana Zaric and Richard Barrett. The presence of Barrett is particularly intriguing, as he pioneered improvised electronic music beginning in the 1990s – largely through FURT, his partnership with Paul Obermayer – laying groundwork for Wright and others. Additionally, Barrett’s compositions are renowned for testing – and often surpassing – the presumed physical limits of instrumentalists. Barrett and Wright are part of a trajectory of composers foregrounding technology in their work. An earlier dot on the line, one that is essential but not obvious, is Conlon Nancarrow. The expatriate composer is the inspiration for Wright’s next major work, “Passing Nancarrow.” Wright’s latest project with the Belgian ensemble BI!NDMAN (the exclamation point is intentional) also has Hawkins in a key role. The piece debuts next year, marking 30 years since Nancarrow died. “The idea of the piece is based around Nancarrow being obsessed with Art Tatum’s playing,” Wright explained. “He sampled Tatum in the form of piano rolls, using technology from a hundred years ago. What we will do is, while Alex plays in real time, his notes are captured and triggers all sorts of reactions from the group. In a way, we turn his music into a piano roll.” Wright was partly inspired by the writer and documentary film director Helen Borton’s comment that jazz and blues collide like a “hurricane” in Nancarrow’s music. Replace “hurricane” with “Nancarrow” and you get the gist of Wright’s conceptualization for the piece – “four hurricanes of all kinds of crazy sounds.” Wright also considered the music of Squarepusher, Aphex Twin, and other exponents of electronic dance music, that influenced him when Nancarrow died in 1997, leading him to include “strange, intelligent dance music in the piece.” However, the nexus of Nancarrow, Barrett, and Wright, is the consideration of the limits of music humans can create in real time, and how to get to the edge of those limits, if not extend them. “Nancarrow reached for the impossible. I don’t currently have an interest in AI. I’ve heard a lot of AI stuff in my job as an academic. I hear a lot of AI research. The thing I’m not interested in is that AI can do anything. In a way, doing anything is boring when you don’t hear the labor. In Alex’s playing, there is that reaching beyond what is supposedly humanly possible and reach a new vista for what is possible. “You can say that, for his times, Nancarrow was making a post-human kind of music, but we should remember that he sat there, punching holes. So, I don’t hear a sort of pre-AI in his music, a piano that can do anything, but the blood and the hours of Nancarrow sitting maybe six months to create an explosive two minutes. I want to know how humans feel when they hear music and when they make music. If that is aided by technology, the idea is that the technology helps like an instrument helps. My interest in technology is the same as Alex’s interest in the piano, that there’s a tradition there. “Another thing I like about Nancarrow was that he was true to his beliefs, which is why he left the US for Mexico City, which resulted in him working in relative isolation. He just got on with it. A few people had experimented with the piano before, but he made it his own. I appreciate that you can hear the edges in music and you’re OK with not being able to know everything beyond that edge. I guess the difference between the scene we have now and Nancarrow’s situation is that we can go to the edge together in a collaborative spirit.”
